title: Early Environmental Shocks and Organizational Reconfiguration in High-Growth Ventures
authors: Sunasir Dutta; Pyung Nahm; Luis Adrian Rios
affiliations: University of Minnesota Carlson School of Management, Strategic Management and Entrepreneurship, Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States; University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Carlson School of Management, Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States; Purdue University Krannert School of Management, Strategic Management, West Lafayette, Indiana, United States
abstract: We study whether shocks from local natural disasters can leave durable organizational traces in young high-growth ventures. In principle, such firms may be relatively resilient to localized disruption because they are designed to scale beyond local markets and rely heavily on knowledge-based assets. We examine this possibility using a panel of 19,984 U.S. startups founded between 1985 and 2010 that subsequently received venture financing. We identify ventures whose founding counties experience natural disasters within 12 months of founding using FEMA Major Disaster Declarations. Ventures exposed to disasters at an early stage exhibit higher subsequent failure hazards and no general advantage in follow-on financing, yet show higher IPO hazards in favorable market windows, a pattern consistent with greater responsiveness to opportunities requiring substantial organizational reconfiguration. Descriptive employee-level evidence further documents differences in organizational structure and composition consistent with greater retained fluidity among exposed ventures. Drawing on organization design and imprinting theory, we interpret these patterns as consistent with the possibility that disasters function as forcing environments that entrench early-stage coordination features such as flatness, role fluidity, and broader expertise that would otherwise attenuate as ventures mature. These durable organizational traces may, in turn, shape ventures’ subsequent capacity for reconfiguration. We discuss implications for organizational adaptation, imprinting, entrepreneurial geography, and organizational responses to crises.

title: Planning Stormwater Retention for Resilience Against Extreme Rainfalls
authors: Sheng Liu; Wei Qi; Aiqi Zhang
affiliations: Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 3E6 Canada; Department of Industrial Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China; Lazaridis School of Business and Economics, Wilfrid Laurier University, Waterloo, Ontario N2L 3C7, Canada
abstract: Rethinking How Cities Prepare for Extreme Rainfall Cities often prepare for extreme rainfall using a single “design storm,” such as a 100-year storm of a predetermined duration. But storms with the same return period can produce very different flooding losses. In “Planning Stormwater Retention for Resilience Against Extreme Rainfalls,” Liu, Qi, and Zhang develop a robust optimization framework that identifies the most damaging rainfall scenario for a city based on its existing drainage and retention infrastructure. Case studies of Toronto, Manhattan, and New Orleans show that the storm a city should prepare for changes with local infrastructure and climate conditions. The analysis also challenges the idea that greener is always more resilient; although green infrastructure offers important environmental benefits, concentrated gray infrastructure can become more valuable when rainfall is severe or budgets are tight. In Toronto, robust planning could save an estimated $6 million annually today and as much as $1.5 billion annually by 2050.

title: The Welfare Effects of Selling Leads in a Two-Sided Marketplace
authors: Peng Shi
affiliations: USC Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089
abstract: Digital platforms that connect customers with service providers often monetize by selling customer leads to interested providers. Examples include Bark, Google Local Services, HomeAdvisor, Modernize, Porch, and Thumbtack. This paper develops a game-theoretic model to analyze how lead pricing affects customer and provider welfare. When the platform raises the fee-per-lead for a customer-type, those customers—conditional on receiving the same number of provider quotes—are quoted lower prices. However, if the fee is sufficiently high, providers purchase fewer of these leads, which can reduce the number of quotes and diminish customer surplus. To maximize social welfare, a simple policy that sets a market-clearing fee-per-lead for each customer-type guarantees at least [Formula: see text] of the first-best welfare and at least [Formula: see text] of the welfare under the welfare-optimal fees. The first-best outcome can be achieved by subsidizing providers for each job well done, so that experienced providers with cheaper sources of leads do not exit the platform. Understanding these welfare trade-offs can help platforms design policies that support balanced marketplace growth and preserve a sustainable revenue stream. title: Facade of Trust: The Impact of Adopting AI-Enhanced Profile Pictures on Trust
authors: Sijia Ma; Chong (Alex) Wang; Xiaoquan (Michael) Zhang; Tao Lu
affiliations: Tilburg University Tilburg School of Economics and Management, Department of Management, Tilburg, 5037 AB, Netherlands; Peking University, Information Systems, Beijing, Beijing, China; Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decision Sciences and Managerial Economics, Shatin, N.T., CUHK Business School, Hong Kong; Southern University of Science and Technology, Information Systems, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China
abstract: Virtual profiles are critical elements of online social interactions, often featuring portraits enhanced by AI-driven tools such as beauty filters and virtual makeup. While the increasing use of these technologies reshapes how individuals present and perceive themselves, little is known about their implications for trust-related behavior. Drawing on self-presentation theory, this study examines how adopting an enhanced profile photo influences behavioral trust and trustworthiness toward others. We conducted a randomized experiment based on the trust game and adapted it by embedding a novel profile photo enhancement module. Participants were assigned to either a treatment group, in which they adopted an AI-enhanced profile photo, or a control group, in which they used their original photo. Our findings reveal an intriguing asymmetry. Senders with an enhanced photo demonstrated less trust by sending smaller amounts. Conversely, receivers with an enhanced photo displayed greater trustworthiness, returning higher percentages. These effects were offset when participants were interacting with an opponent using an enhanced photo. Further analysis indicates that enhanced self-presentation increases perceived risk, which explains the observed reduction in trust. We also document gender differences: female senders show a larger decline in trust, while male receivers exhibit a greater increase in trustworthiness. Overall, this research highlights the asymmetric behavioral consequences of AI-powered self-presentation and underscores the role of risk perception in linking profile photo enhancement to trust behavior in online interactions.

title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce
authors: Qili Wang; Yi SU; Liangfei Qiu; Runyu Chen
affiliations: University of Florida Warrington College of Business, Department of Information Systems and Operations Management, Gainesville, Florida, United States; University of Florida, ISOM, Gainesville, Florida, United States; University of Florida, Department of Information Systems and Operations Management, Gainesville, Florida, United States; University of International Business and Economics, e-commerce, Beijing, China
abstract: Amidst the burgeoning incorporation of generative AI into commercial realms, numerous companies are exploring ways to leverage generative AI tools in practice. However, there is still a lack of empirical evidence to examine their effectiveness. In this research, we explore how AI-generated summaries (AIGS), a relatively new generative AI tool, influence consumer review behavior. While one may assume that AI-generated content diminishes users’ incentive to contribute by replacing user-generated content, we find the opposite: the introduction of AIGS actually leads to an increase in the volume of consumer reviews. We propose that this effect is driven by enhanced perceptions of collective efficacy. By highlighting the value of consumer reviews as a collective force, AIGS reinforces contributors’ belief that their individual input meaningfully contributes to a shared body of product knowledge, thus motivating participation. This mechanism is supported by an additional controlled laboratory experiment where we directly measure perceived collective efficacy and find that it mediates the effect of AIGS on the likelihood of leaving a review. Our moderation analysis results reveal that the positive effect of AIGS on review contributions is more pronounced among products that are well-reviewed (vs. under-reviewed) and polarizing (vs. non-polarizing). Moreover, a fine-grained review content analysis shows that reviews after the AIGS introduction exhibit enhanced content richness and provide complementary information beyond the AIGS content. Specifically, contributors discuss fewer product attributes already covered by AIGS, discuss more product attributes not covered by AIGS, and elaborate on AIGS product attributes rather than restating the summary. Taken together, these findings advance our understanding of how AI integration influences consumer review behaviors in e-commerce and offer valuable practical guidance for business strategies on employing generative AI.

title: Mapping Interactions Within EU Food and Feed Risk Analysis: A Comparative Study of Risk Assessors and Risk Managers
authors: Axel Menning; Leonie Dendler; Joao Borges; Anneluise Mader; Mats Gunnar Andersson
affiliations: German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) Berlin Germany; Wageningen University Wageningen the Netherlands; National Veterinary Institute (SVA) Uppsala Sweden
abstract: ABSTRACT Considering prominent calls for various forms of cooperation, coordination, and collaboration within risk analysis processes, this empirical research study aims to delineate current forms of interaction between risk assessors and risk managers. Utilizing an online survey, it analyses responses from 95 professionals working in the field of food and feed risk analysis across at least 23 EU countries and determines interaction scores based on the degree of cooperation, coordination, and collaboration. The scores show that current interaction dominantly aligns with cooperation across multiple dimensions. However, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) reveals significant perceptual differences between risk assessors and managers regarding their mutual interaction. In particular, risk assessors perceive their interaction with risk management more cooperative and risk managers perceive their interaction with risk assessment more collaborative. A notable difference was also observed in the interaction scores for routine risk analysis versus rapid risk analysis. In addition, clustering analysis and regression analysis was conducted to examine the relation and impact of different interaction dimensions on perceived quality of risk analysis. While the results do not support uniform calls for more collaboration, they show positive effects of open and frequent communication on the perceived quality of risk analysis. These results suggest working towards more individualized and fit‐for‐purpose interactions as well as to extend practitioner‐oriented dialogue on desired modes of interactions, to enhance mutual understanding in their collective risk analysis.

title: Theorizing Cross‐Boundary Strategizing as Situated in Multilayered Supply Chains: A Strategy‐as‐Practice Approach to Supply Chain Management
authors: Qian Li; Julia Grimm; Paula Jarzabkowski
affiliations: Warwick Business School University of Warwick Coventry UK; Stockholm Business School Stockholm University Stockholm Sweden; House of Sustainable Society Stockholm School of Economics Stockholm Sweden; UQ Business School University of Queensland St Lucia Australia; Bayes Business School City St George's, University of London London UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Supply chain strategy is increasingly recognized as a multilayered phenomenon, with firms strategizing not only within their own boundaries but across supply chain tiers, jurisdictions, and wider regulatory and ecological systems. Yet most existing supply chain management research tends to treat these tiers, jurisdictions, and systems as contexts for strategizing rather than as something strategizing helps to constitute, leaving the cross‐boundary character undertheorized. This article introduces the strategy‐as‐practice (SAP) lens as an epistemic tool for theorizing cross‐boundary strategizing in multilayered supply chains. Drawing on SAP's tripartite framework of practices, practitioners, and praxis (three Ps), we show that strategizing is inherently cross‐boundary, both implicitly through the knowledge practitioners draw on beyond their organization and explicitly through direct interaction with counterparts in other firms and institutions. We introduce three approaches SAP scholars use to conceptualize the complex systems within which strategizing is situated: a “tall” ontology separating intraorganizational from extraorganizational practice, a “flat” ontology treating strategizing as a web of practices stretching sideways, and a zoom‐in/zoom‐out approach tracing connectivity and identifying consequentiality across layers. Using a heuristic case of a European solar company and its Chinese supplier network, we show how each approach can shape the research orientation and theoretical payoff. We close with a research agenda for cross‐boundary strategizing in supply chains and argue that supply chains have the potential to extend SAP's own theoretical apparatus.

title: Business Model Bundles: Implications for Innovation in the Circular Economy
authors: Miying Yang; Steve Evans
affiliations: School of Management Cranfield University Bedford UK; Institute for Manufacturing University of Cambridge Cambridge UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Business model (BM) innovation is essential to the transition towards a circular economy, yet customers often resist circular BMs. This study investigates how manufacturers can innovate BMs for circularity in ways that increase customer acceptance. Drawing on a multiple‐case study of four manufacturers offering 21 product‐service system BMs, we introduce a new concept, the business model bundle: a strategic offering that packages multiple BMs within one contract and gives customers flexibility to move between them over time. We identify three defining characteristics: the combination of different BMs, contractual flexibility, and temporal transition. We theorize the BM bundle as a new form of BM innovation that creates, delivers, and captures value through the configuration of existing BMs rather than the invention of new ones. Our evidence indicates that the flexibility offered by BM bundles can reduce customers' initial commitment and make previously resisted circular BMs more acceptable. However, bundles may lead towards either greater or lesser circularity and therefore require deliberate design. The study extends innovation management and BM research by introducing the BM bundle that could open a new avenue in the field of BM innovation, and by identifying flexibility as a mechanism linking BM bundles to firm‐perceived customer acceptance.

title: Union Strength, Collective Bargaining, and Strike Activity: Insights From Chile's 2017 Labor Reform
authors: Martín Dibarrart; Esteban Puentes; Tomás Rau
affiliations: University of Minnesota Minneapolis Minnesota USA; Department of Economics Universidad de Chile Santiago Chile; Instituto de Economía Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile and IZA Santiago Chile
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the causal impact of Chile's 2017 labor reform—which banned the replacement of striking workers and restricted unilateral extension of collective benefits—on strike activity, wages, and employment. Using administrative data on all regulated collective negotiations from 2008 to 2024 in a difference‐in‐differences framework that exploits pre‐reform variation in union density, we find no increase in strike incidence and modest decreases in strike voting and actual stoppages among more unionized firms. Effects on wages are negligible; effects on employment are positive but display pre‐reform trends. The pattern is consistent with the joint cost model and with the institutional‐context literature.

title: How Brokers Enable Collective Identity Formation in Fragmented Industry Groups: The Case of Franciacorta Wineries
authors: Alessandra Zamparini; Ileana Stigliani; Kevin G. Corley
affiliations: Università della Svizzera italiana (USI); Imperial College Business School
abstract: Abstract This study illuminates the role of brokers, that is, actors spanning inter‐organizational boundaries, in the process of collective identity formation in fragmented industry groups. Through an in‐depth longitudinal analysis of the Franciacorta wineries from the 1960s to the 1990s, we uncover how technical consultants acting as brokers facilitated collective identity formation by interacting with wineries through three mechanisms: translation, cross‐pollination, and integration. Our grounded model of collective identity formation reveals a distributed and co‐creative pathway to cohesive identity understandings built from the interstices of fragmented industry groups, through the co‐creation of practices, the weaving of social connections, and the facilitation of an optimally distinctive collective identity via inward adaptation and outward alignment between broader industry domains and local contexts. Our study advances theory by foregrounding the more inconspicuous practice‐level and social work that precedes, and ultimately determines the success of, the more visible identity‐defining moments that happen via symbolic representation or institutional codification.

title:
Financing Risk in Infrastructure
                    <scp>FDI</scp>
                    : A Property Rights Perspective
authors: Rajeev J. Sawant; Barclay E. James
affiliations: Florida Atlantic University; St. Mary's University
abstract: Abstract Property rights theory (PRT) focuses on how allocation of residual control rights of ownership resolves incentive problems from incomplete contracts. However, when asset ownership is efficient for a transacting party, PRT ignores financial resource constraints preventing the party from purchasing it. We include creditors, who provide financial resources but are exposed to agency conflicts with equity‐owners, in property rights analysis. Multinational enterprises (MNEs) reduce agency conflict with creditors through contractual covenants and collateral. Yet contracts are incomplete. Under incomplete contracts, how do MNEs mitigate financing risk, the risk that supply of capital from creditors is delayed or entirely unavailable? We distinguish between incomplete contracts arising from weak property rights institutions and weak contracting institutions. We theorize that allocation of specified control rights through operating and maintenance (O&M) contracts to MNE‐owners mitigates financing risk in countries with weak property rights institutions because MNE‐owners possess high‐powered incentives to exert requisite effort to adapt operations to unexpected contingencies. In contrast, such allocation of O&M contracts to MNE‐owners increases financing risk in countries with weak contracting institutions because such allocation increases agency conflict between MNE‐owners and creditors. Empirical analyses of 363 project‐financed investments in 52 countries worth US$1.53 trillion over 1990–2018 support our theory.

title: Re‐thinking academic entrepreneurship: Micro, meso, and macro perspectives
authors: Maribel Guerrero; Donald Siegel; Mirjam Knockaert; Phillip Phan; Miriam Erez
affiliations: School of Public Affairs, Global Center for Technology Transfer Arizona State University Tempe Arizona USA; Faculty of Economics and Business Administration Ghent University Ghent Belgium; Carey School of Business Johns Hopkins University Baltimore Maryland USA; Faculty of Industrial Engineering and Management Technion‐Israel Institute of Technology Haifa Israel
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We summarize and synthesize the papers contained in the special issue and use these studies to illustrate key micro, meso, and macro dimensions of academic entrepreneurship, where micro focuses on the scientist, meso is concerned with the university ecosystem, and macro refers to the broader entrepreneurial ecosystem. A key finding from our special issue is that routines, pivots, and intellectual property, which determine venture viability, emerge from granular individual action, including identity formation and evolution. We also find that macro instruments such as public funding/grants and institutional governance appear to steer resources toward viable science‐based ventures. Our essay concludes by presenting numerous additional micro, meso, and macro research questions to motivate future research on the managerial and public policy implications of academic entrepreneurship. Managerial Summary There are several key managerial implications of our essay and this special issue. “Managers” and those who supervise academic entrepreneurs need to develop and support their scientists entrepreneurial identity formation and evolution. Managers also need to enhance incentives for academic entrepreneurship and foster a culture within their academic departments, schools, and colleges that support these activities. Policymakers need to design entrepreneurial training for scientists with both “micro” and “macro” issues in mind.

title: Crime and Participation
authors: DAVID DOHERTY; G. AGUSTIN MARKARIAN; MENA WHALEN; DANA GARBARSKI
affiliations: Loyola University Chicago
abstract: Does exposure to crime mobilize or demobilize political participation? We report findings from a preregistered design, leveraging data from an original survey of 21 major U.S. cities and five waves of the Cooperative Election Study. We assess the relationships between direct victimization, local (ZCTA-level) crime rates, and perceived neighborhood safety and two outcomes: turnout (including validated turnout) and non-electoral participation. We find that direct victimization is significantly associated with more non-electoral engagement but lower turnout. The negative estimated effects of victimization on turnout exceed the magnitude of positive effects associated with common get-out-the-vote efforts. We find only limited evidence that crime rates are associated with participation. Perceived neighborhood safety is associated with higher rates of non-electoral, but not electoral, participation. Our findings offer new, comprehensive evidence on the relationship between crime exposure and political participation and illustrate the importance of distinguishing between types of exposure and forms of participation.
